**What to do:** Object to the $500 claim in writing, and do it soon. Don't wait.

**Why the deadline matters.** Under § 83.49(3)(b), if you don't object "within 15 days after receipt of the landlord's notice," the landlord may deduct his claim. He must then send you the balance. Missing the deadline doesn't end your rights. The statute says a late objection "does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." Objecting on time is still the safer course.

**Your deadline.** You told me the letter came today, and I've noted that as the day you received it. I can't count the 15 days until you confirm that date in the sidebar. Please confirm it so I can give you your last day to object.

**How to object.**
- Put it in writing. Say you dispute the $500 claim, and say you want the rest of the deposit returned.
- Send it to the landlord's address in your lease, § 7: Suite A, 1840 SW 13th Street, Gainesville, FL 32608. Section 7 says to deliver written notices to the landlord "by hand" at the office or send them there "by certified mail." Use one of those two methods and keep proof.
- The notice should also tell you where to send your objection, so check the letter for that.

**Is his notice valid?** I can't say yet, because it depends on two things I don't know.
- **How it was sent.** The statute requires "certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505" (§ 83.49(3)(a)). Your lease, § 8, says you and the landlord haven't agreed to e-mail notices. A letter sent some other way, such as regular mail, is unsettled. One reading is that it isn't the required notice, so he loses the right to make a claim on the deposit. The other reading is that a notice you actually received in time is enough, because § 83.505(6) doesn't "preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." Under that reading the claim stands, and you can still dispute whether it's justified.
- **Whether it came in time.** The landlord has 30 days after the rental agreement ends. Counted from your lease end date, that runs to 2026-08-30. Counted from your move-out date, it runs to 2026-08-29. Today is 2026-08-20, so the letter is within time on either count.

**Your early move-out.** You left on 2026-07-30, one day before the lease ended. Section 83.49(5) says a tenant who leaves before the end of the term must give 7 days' written notice, by certified mail or hand delivery, with an address where you can be reached. If you didn't, the landlord doesn't have to follow the notice rule in (3)(a). That doesn't cost you the deposit. The statute says it "does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." So you can still dispute the $500 either way.

**If this goes to court.** The winner gets "court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney" (§ 83.49(3)(c)). That applies only if one side files a lawsuit.

Please answer these two questions:
1. How did the letter reach you (certified mail, regular mail, left at your door, or something else), and what date is printed on it?
2. Can you confirm in the sidebar that you received it today?

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

**What to do: object in writing, and do it soon.** Under 83.49(3)(b), if you don't object to the claim or its amount within 15 days after you receive the notice, the landlord may deduct it. You can object to the claim, the amount, or both. If you miss the deadline, you can still sue later for a refund.

I've noted that you received the letter today, 2026-08-20. Please confirm that date in the sidebar. Once you do, I can give you the exact last day to object.

**Is the landlord's notice valid?** The answer depends on two things I don't know yet.

1. **How the letter was sent.** Under 83.49(3)(a), a claim notice must go "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505." Your lease says the parties have not agreed to e-mail notices (lease §8), so e-mail wouldn't count. If the letter came by regular mail or was hand-delivered, there are two readings.
   - **Reading 1:** It isn't the required notice, so the landlord loses the right to claim anything and owes you the full $1,050. The statute says a landlord who doesn't give the required notice "forfeits the right to impose a claim."
   - **Reading 2:** A notice you actually received in time is enough, because 83.505(6) says it "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." The claim then stands, subject to your objection.

2. **Whether the landlord was excused from giving notice.**
   - **Timing:** You moved out on 2026-07-30, one day before your lease ended on 2026-07-31. Under 83.49(5), a tenant who leaves before the end of the term must give at least 7 days' written notice. The notice must go "by certified mail or personal delivery," and it must include an address where you can be reached. Your lease doesn't set a different rule.
   - **Deadline:** The 7-day deadline was 2026-07-23, and it has passed. Emailing your forwarding address on 2026-07-30 doesn't meet that requirement.
   - **If you gave no earlier notice:** The landlord is relieved of the notice requirement. The statute says that doesn't waive "any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." The landlord's claim would still have to be a real one, and you can still dispute it.

**Timing of the landlord's notice:** The 30-day window hasn't closed yet. It runs to 2026-08-29 if it counts from your move-out, or 2026-08-30 if it counts from the lease end. So this letter came inside the window on either reading. If it was properly sent, the late-notice forfeiture wouldn't apply.

- Write down your objection. Say you dispute the $500 claim and the reason (for example, that the carpet was left clean or the amount is excessive). The notice form tells you to send it to the landlord's address in the letter.
- Lease §7 says written notices to the landlord go by hand to Suite A, 1840 SW 13th Street, or by certified mail. Using one of those is the safest way to show you objected.
- The landlord must send you the balance within 30 days after the date on the notice.
- If someone sues over the deposit, 83.49(3)(c) gives the winner court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

If you disagree with the $500, send the landlord a written objection now. The 15-day clock for that runs from the day you received the letter.

**Why the objection matters**
- Under 83.49(3)(b), if you don't object within "15 days after receipt of the landlord's notice," the landlord "may then deduct the amount of his or her claim." He must then send you the rest of the deposit within 30 days after the date of his notice.
- If you do object, he can't simply deduct the $500.
- Not objecting doesn't end your rights. 83.49(3)(b) says a late objection "does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action."

**Where things stand**
- You received the letter today, 2026-08-20. I've noted that as your receipt date. Please confirm it in the sidebar. Once you do, I'll count your last day to object.
- Neither 30-day window has run out. Counting from your lease end, it runs to 2026-08-30. Counting from your move-out date, it runs to 2026-08-29. So a claim notice sent in this window isn't late.
- You moved out on 2026-07-30, one day before the lease ended on 2026-07-31. Under 83.49(5), a tenant who leaves before the term ends must give 7 days' written notice by certified mail or hand delivery. Without that notice, the landlord is relieved of the 30-day notice requirement. That could matter if the claim notice turned out to be defective. Even then, 83.49(5) says you keep your right to the deposit.

**How to object**
- Put it in writing. Say you object to the $500 carpet-cleaning deduction and want it returned.
- Under lease §7, written notices to the landlord must be hand-delivered to "1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or sent there by certified mail. The statute's form notice also says to send the objection to the landlord's address. Email isn't a delivery method under the lease, so don't rely on it.
- Keep a copy and proof of delivery, such as a certified mail receipt.

**Two things I can't tell from here**
- **How the letter came.** 83.49(3)(a) requires certified mail to your last known address, or email under a signed addendum. Your lease says in §8 that you didn't agree to email notices. A letter sent some other way, such as regular mail, is an open question.
  - One reading is that it isn't the required notice, so the landlord forfeits the claim and owes the full $1,050.
  - The other reading is that a notice you actually received in time is enough, since 83.505(6) says it "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law."
  - Either way, you should still object within the 15 days.
- **Whether you gave 7 days' written notice before leaving.** See the 83.49(5) point above.

If this goes to court, 83.49(3)(c) gives the winning side its court costs and a reasonable attorney fee. It applies only if someone files suit.
